title: Digital options and call spreads
objectives: Price a digital as a tight call spread and as $e^{-rT}N(d_2)$.
Split a call into digitals and size a digital's hedge near expiry

screens.title: A bet from calls
screens.prose: Interviewer: price a bet that pays £1 if the share ends above 100. Hint: you may trade calls. Buy the call at $100 - h/2$, sell the call at $100 + h/2$, and divide the payoff by $h$. Shrink $h$.

state.caption: Payoff of the call spread divided by its width h. Rates are 5% on this lesson.

screens.question: As $h$ shrinks, the scaled spread becomes what?

options.text: A step: £0 below 100 and £1 above, the digital

options.why: You watched the ramp get narrower and missed that its top stays at 1. Only its width shrinks.

options.text: The call's payoff, a straight line above 100
options.why: You kept the call's slope. Selling the higher call caps the payoff at 1 after dividing by $h$.

feedback.correct: The ramp from 0 to 1 gets steeper until it is the step.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide $h$ to 1 and compare with the dashed step.

explain.text: The ramp runs from 0 to 1 over a width $h$. As $h \to 0$ it becomes the step, which pays £1 above the strike: a digital call.

screens.title: Price the bet
screens.prose: These are one-year call prices ($S = 100$, $\sigma = 20\%$, $r = 5\%$). Buy the 99.5 call and sell the 100.5 call: the spread has width 1, so divide its cost by 1.
screens.question: What does the scaled spread cost?

hints.text: Buy the lower strike and sell the higher one.
Subtract the two highlighted prices.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the price of the 100.5 call from the price of the 99.5 call.

byKey.unscaled-width: You used the wide 95 and 105 strikes, a spread of width 10, and divided by nothing. Its value is 5.325 for a width of 10, so scale by 10 to 0.5325.

explain.text: The spread pays at most £1 over a width of £1, so £0.5323 is the price of the bet to four places. Wider spreads give 0.5325 at width 10 and 0.5330 at width 20: the limit is 0.5323.

screens.title: Name the limit
screens.prose: As $h \to 0$ the scaled spread is $-\partial C/\partial K$, the slope of the call price against the strike. It equals the digital call, $e^{-rT}\Phi(d_2)$. Here $d_2 = 0.15$, $\Phi(0.15) = 0.5596$ and $e^{-0.05} = 0.9512$.
screens.question: Compute the digital call's price.

hints.text: Multiply the discount factor by $\Phi(d_2)$.

feedback.correct: About 53p: the discounted chance of finishing above 100.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Discount $\Phi(d_2)$ for one year at 5%.

byKey.no-discount: You left out $e^{-rT}$. The £1 arrives at expiry, so today it is worth less.
byKey.d1-slip: You used $\Phi(d_1)$, which is the call's delta. The digital needs $\Phi(d_2)$.

explain.text: The slope of $C$ against $K$ is $-e^{-rT}\Phi(d_2)$, so the scaled spread tends to $0.9512 \times 0.5596 = 0.5323$. The limit matches the width-0.1 spread, 0.532325.

screens.title: The digital put
screens.prose: A digital put pays £1 if the share ends below 100. Together the call and the put pay £1 in every case. Use $\Phi(-0.15) = 0.4404$.
screens.question: What is the digital put's price?

hints.text: Discount the chance of finishing below the strike.
That chance is $\Phi(-d_2)$.

feedback.correct: The put is worth £0.4189, and the pair sums to £0.9512.

byKey.one-minus-call: You took 1 minus the call, which forgets the discount. The two bets sum to £0.9512, not £1.

explain.text: Call plus put is $0.5323 + 0.4189 = 0.9512 = e^{-rT}$: £1 for sure, paid at $T$. Say that aloud as a check.

screens.title: The call as two digitals
screens.prose: Put the lines in order. Interviewers write $N(d_2)$ for $\Phi(d_2)$: it is the same normal cdf.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: The call pays $(S_T - K)\,\mathbf 1\{S_T > K\} = S_T\,\mathbf 1\{S_T > K\} - K\,\mathbf 1\{S_T > K\}$, since it pays nothing below $K$
The $K$ piece is $K$ digitals, worth $Ke^{-rT}\Phi(d_2) = 100 \times 0.5323 = 53.23$, from the digital's price
The $S_T$ piece is an asset-or-nothing option, worth $S\Phi(d_1) = 100 \times 0.6368 = 63.68$, the share's own risk-neutral weight
Subtract: $63.68 - 53.23 = 10.45$, which is the formula $S\Phi(d_1) - Ke^{-rT}\Phi(d_2)$ of lesson 10

hints.text: Split the payoff at the strike first.
The two pieces can be priced in either order.
Split, price the two pieces, then subtract.

feedback.correct: The call is an asset-or-nothing option less $K$ digitals.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split the payoff, price each piece, then subtract.

byKey.d: You subtracted before pricing the two pieces. Price them first.

explain.text: Black-Scholes is two digitals in disguise: $S\Phi(d_1)$ for the share leg and $Ke^{-rT}\Phi(d_2)$ for the cash leg. Interviewers write $N(d_1)$ and $N(d_2)$ for the same two numbers.

screens.title: The chance of finishing in the money
screens.prose: A candidate says: the digital's price is the chance of finishing in the money. The share is at £100 with a 100 strike and a 5% rate.
screens.question: What is the digital's price, in words?

options.text: The discounted risk-neutral chance, $e^{-rT}\Phi(d_2)$, with the share growing at $r$
The real-world chance that the share ends above 100
options.why: You used the real-world chance. A trade is priced by the hedge, and the hedge uses risk-neutral probabilities.
You used $\Phi(d_1)$, the call's delta. It weights the share, not the £1.
You left out the discount. The £1 arrives at $T$, so today it is worth 95p.

hints.text: Which chance does the hedge use?
The call spread pays £1 above the strike whatever the real-world chance is.
Risk-neutral chance times the discount factor.

feedback.correct: Price is the discounted risk-neutral chance.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The hedge fixes the price, not the share's real drift.

byKey.real: You used the real-world chance. Our hedge never uses it.
byKey.d1: Φ(d₁) is the call's delta, 0.6368. The digital is 0.5323.

explain.text: The risk-neutral chance of finishing above 100 is $\Phi(d_2) = 0.5596$, since the share grows at $r$. The price is that times $e^{-rT}$, 0.5323.

screens.title: A hedge that always pays
screens.prose: A dealer sells the digital call and wants a hedge that pays at least £1 whenever the digital pays. Buy the 99 call and sell the 100 call, scaled by 1. Prices: £10.9923 and £10.4506.

state.caption: The spread lies on or above the bet at every price.

screens.question: What does this safe hedge cost?

hints.text: Buy the lower strike and sell the higher one.
Subtract the two prices.

feedback.correct: The safe hedge costs 54p against a fair 53p.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the 100 call's price from the 99 call's.

byKey.fair-price: You gave the digital's fair price. The hedge that always pays costs more.

explain.text: The spread pays £1 from 100 up and part of £1 between 99 and 100, so it always covers the sold digital. It costs £0.0094 more than fair: that is the price of safety.

screens.title: Pin risk
screens.prose: Edge case. A digital's delta is $e^{-rT}\varphi(d_2)/(S\sigma\sqrt T)$. The curve shows shares to hold against 10,000 digitals, one year out and one trading day out. Share at £100.
screens.question: How many shares do you hold against 10,000 digitals one day from expiry, at the strike?

hints.text: Put $T = 1/252$ and $\varphi(d_2) \approx 0.3989$ into the delta.
$S\sigma\sqrt T = 100 \times 0.2 \times 0.063 = 1.26$.

feedback.correct: About 3,166 shares: a huge delta in a tiny range.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $T = 1/252$ and scale to 10,000 digitals.

byKey.year: You used one year, 188 shares. One day out the delta is far larger.
byKey.per-one: You gave the delta of one digital. The book holds 10,000.

explain.text: One day out the delta is 0.3166 a digital, or 3,166 for the book, against 188 a year out. A digital near expiry is a huge delta in a tiny range, so a small move changes the hedge by thousands of shares.

screens.title: A client's note
screens.prose: Interviewer: a client buys £2m notional of a one-year digital call struck at 100. It pays £1 per £1 of notional if the index ends above 100. Index 100, vol 20%, rate 5%. About 90 seconds: reason first, then the price.
screens.question: What does the note cost?

hints.text: Price per £1, then scale by the notional.
The digital call is worth 0.532325 per £1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the digital's price by £2m.

byKey.no-discount: You used Φ(d₂) without the discount, 0.5596. The payout comes in a year.
byKey.d1-slip: You used Φ(d₁), the call's delta, 0.6058 with the discount. The note needs Φ(d₂).

explain.text: The note costs $2{,}000{,}000 \times 0.532325 = £1{,}064{,}650$. Say aloud: discount times the chance it finishes in the money, about 53p.

screens.title: The digital in code
screens.prose: Interviewer: price it two ways. `digital_call` and `digital_put` use the formula with $d_2$. `spread_digital` prices the scaled call spread, using the supplied `bs_call`.
screens.question: Complete the three functions.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests. Prices match to 5 places, and the spread to within 1e-5 of the formula.

hints.text: $d_2 = (\ln(S/K) + (r - \sigma^2/2)T)/(\sigma\sqrt T)$.
The digital put uses $\Phi(-d_2)$, discounted the same way.
The spread is the lower call less the higher call, divided by $h$.

feedback.correct: The formula and the spread agree to five places.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check $d_2$, the discount factor and the order of the two strikes.

explain.text: The spread converges to the formula as $h$ shrinks: 0.532327 at $h = 1$ and 0.532325 at $h = 0.01$. In practice a desk trades the spread, because it cannot trade a true step.

ideas: A digital call is the limit of a call spread divided by its width, which is $-\partial C/\partial K$.
Its price is $e^{-rT}\Phi(d_2)$: the discounted risk-neutral chance of finishing in the money, 0.5323 here, and call plus put is $e^{-rT}$.
A call is an asset-or-nothing option less $K$ digitals, and a digital's delta explodes near expiry.

formula.name: Digital call
formula.note: Pays £1 if S_T > K; interviewers write N(d_2).

summary.trap: The digital's price is not the chance of finishing in the money: discount it, and use the risk-neutral chance.

quiz.prose: The shared option: S = 100, σ = 20%, r = 5%, T = 1. The digital call at strike 105 is worth £0.4400.
quiz.question: What is the digital put at strike 105?

feedback.correct: The pair sums to the discount factor, 0.9512, so the put is £0.5112.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Call plus put is the discount factor, 0.9512.

byKey.call: You gave the call's price. The put is the rest of the discounted £1.
byKey.no-discount: You used Φ(−d₂) without the discount. Multiply by 0.9512.

quiz.prose: A digital call and a digital put share a strike, expiry and share.
quiz.question: What do their prices sum to?

options.text: The discount factor $e^{-rT}$: £1 for sure, paid at $T$

options.why: You forgot the discount. The £1 arrives at expiry.
You assumed the two chances are one half each. They sum to one, and the price is discounted.

feedback.correct: Exactly one of the two pays £1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. One of the two always pays.

explain.text: One of the two pays £1 at $T$ in every case, so together they are worth $e^{-rT} = 0.9512$.

quiz.prose: An asset-or-nothing call pays the share if it ends above $K$.
quiz.question: What is it less $K$ digital calls?

options.why: You flipped the sign. Below $K$ both pieces pay nothing, so the call is the difference above $K$.
A forward pays $S_T - K$ everywhere. These pieces pay only above $K$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the pieces where $S_T > K$.

explain.text: Above $K$ the difference pays $S_T - K$ and below it pays nothing: a call. Its price is $S\Phi(d_1) - Ke^{-rT}\Phi(d_2)$.

quiz.prose: A dealer sold a digital call and buys the call spread from $K - 1$ to $K$, scaled by 1.
quiz.question: Compared with the digital's fair price, the hedge costs:

options.text: More, since it pays at least £1 whenever the digital does
The same, since both pay £1 above $K$
options.why: You compared payoffs above $K$ only. The spread also pays a part of £1 between $K - 1$ and $K$.

options.text: Less, since a spread is cheaper than a call
options.why: You compared the spread with one call. The comparison is with the digital, which the spread covers.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Does the spread ever pay less than the digital?

explain.text: The spread covers the digital at every price and pays extra between $K - 1$ and $K$. Here it costs £0.5417 against £0.5323.
